lessons.title: Newborn Piglet Processing and Care
lessons.body: When a sow farrows, each piglet needs immediate attention. First, clear mucus from the mouth and nose with a clean cloth. Rub the piglet dry with a soft towel or straw to stimulate breathing and circulation. If a piglet isn't breathing, hold it upside down and gently swing it, or rub its chest. Next, tie the umbilical cord with clean thread about 2 cm from the belly, cut it with sterilized scissors, and dip the stump in iodine. This prevents infection. Keep the farrowing pen at 30-32Â°C for the first week using a heat lamp or a wooden box with a lid and a light bulb. Piglets are born with no fat, so they chill easily. Provide a creep area with dry bedding like wood shavings or rice husks. Within 24 hours, clip needle teeth using clean side-cutters to prevent facial injuries to the sow and other piglets. Also, clip the tips of the eight needle teeth, not the whole tooth. If you plan to castrate males, do it at 3-7 days old with a sharp scalpel and iodine. Ear notch or tag for identification. Weigh each piglet at birth and record. A healthy piglet weighs 1.2-1.8 kg. Any piglet under 1 kg needs extra careâput it on the sow's best teat or supplement with a bottle. Always handle piglets gently and quickly to avoid stress. Wash your hands before and after handling. Keep the pen clean and dry. These steps reduce mortality from 30% to under 10%.

lessons.title: Colostrum Management and Early Nutrition
lessons.body: Colostrum is the first milk a sow produces, rich in antibodies and energy. Piglets are born with no immunity; they must absorb antibodies from colostrum within 6 hours of birth. After 24 hours, their gut closes and antibodies cannot pass. So ensure every piglet suckles within 30 minutes of birth. If a sow has more piglets than teats (common with 12-14 piglets), split-suckle: put half the litter on the sow for 1 hour, then the other half. Or rotate every 2 hours. Weak piglets should be helped onto a teat. The best teats are the front onesâthey give more milk. Attach small piglets to front teats and larger ones to back teats. If a sow dies or rejects a piglet, use a foster sow. Rub the piglet with the foster sow's afterbirth or bedding to mask scent. If no foster sow, feed colostrum from another sow or a commercial colostrum replacer using a bottle or syringe (without needle). Give 20-30 ml per piglet every 2 hours for the first 6 hours. After 24 hours, piglets need regular milk. Sow's milk is best. If the sow is not producing enough, supplement with a milk replacer (e.g., 1 part milk replacer to 4 parts warm water) fed at 28-30Â°C. From day 3, offer a creep feedâa highly digestible pellet with 20-22% protein, 1-2% fibre, and added vitamins. Put a small amount in a shallow tray in the creep area. Change it daily. Piglets will nibble and learn to eat. By 2 weeks, they should be eating 50-100 g per day. Always provide fresh, clean water. Dehydration kills piglets fast. Use shallow bowls so they can drink easily.

lessons.title: Weaning Strategies and Transition Diets
lessons.body: Weaning is the most stressful time for piglets. In Africa, many farmers wean at 4-6 weeks, but early weaning (3-4 weeks) requires excellent hygiene and feed. The goal is to move piglets from milk to solid feed without growth check. Prepare piglets by offering creep feed from day 7. By 3 weeks, they should eat 150-200 g per day. Wean gradually: remove the sow for 2-3 days, then return her for 1 day, then remove permanently. Or use fence-line weaning: keep piglets in the same pen but separate them from the sow with a fence so they can see and smell her. This reduces stress. After weaning, keep piglets in the same pen for 3-5 days to avoid moving stress. Then move to a clean, warm nursery pen. Feed a transition diet for 7-10 days: the same creep feed they were eating, then gradually mix in a nursery diet (18-20% protein). Change feed over 5 days: day 1: 75% creep, 25% nursery; day 3: 50-50; day 5: 25% creep, 75% nursery; day 7: 100% nursery. Feed small amounts 4-6 times a day. Piglets have small stomachs; they cannot eat much at once. Overfeeding causes diarrhoea. Use feeders that allow easy access. Provide clean water always. Add electrolytes to water for the first 3 days after weaning. Keep the nursery at 28-30Â°C for the first week, then reduce by 1Â°C per week until 22Â°C. Good ventilation but no draughts. Weigh piglets weekly and record. If a piglet loses weight, isolate and feed separately. Weaning weight should be 6-8 kg at 4 weeks. With good management, you can wean 10-12 piglets per sow.

lessons.title: Nursery Environment and Comfort
lessons.body: The nursery must be warm, dry, clean, and well-ventilated. Piglets cannot regulate body temperature well. For the first week after weaning, keep the pen at 28-30Â°C. Use a heat lamp (250-watt infrared bulb) hanging 45-60 cm above the floor. Or use a wooden box with a lid and a 100-watt bulb. Provide dry bedding: wood shavings, rice husks, or chopped straw. Never use wet beddingâit grows bacteria. Clean and replace bedding daily. The floor should be non-slip. Concrete is good but must be rough. Smooth floors cause leg injuries. If using slatted floors, gaps should be 10-12 mm wide so piglets don't get stuck. Space: each piglet needs 0.3-0.4 square metres. For 10 piglets, a pen of 3-4 square metres is enough. Ventilation: ammonia from urine burns lungs. You should not smell ammonia when you enter. Open windows or use a ridge vent. Avoid draughtsâpiglets catch cold easily. Use a curtain or wall to block wind. Lighting: 12-16 hours of light helps piglets find feed and water. Use natural light or a bulb. Keep the pen quiet. Loud noises stress piglets. Limit visitors. Always have a hospital pen for sick or small piglets. That pen should be warmer (30-32Â°C) and have soft bedding. Feeders: use a shallow trough or a creep feeder with 5-6 cm of feeding space per piglet. Water: use nipple drinkers or shallow bowls. Check water flow daily. Clean and disinfect the nursery between batches. Use 2% caustic soda or a commercial disinfectant. Let it dry for 2 days before new piglets arrive. This breaks disease cycles.

lessons.title: Managing Piglet Health and Mortality
lessons.body: The first 3 weeks are when most piglets die. Common causes: chilling, starvation, diarrhoea, and crushing by the sow. To prevent crushing, install farrowing railsâmetal or wooden bars 20-25 cm from the wall and 20 cm above the floor. This gives piglets a safe zone when the sow lies down. Also, keep the sow calm. Feed her well before farrowing. For diarrhoea (scours), act fast. A piglet with watery yellow or white stool can die in 12 hours. Isolate it. Give oral rehydration solution: 1 litre clean water, 1 teaspoon salt, 6 teaspoons sugar. Feed 20-30 ml every 2 hours. For bacterial scours, use antibiotics like amoxicillin (follow vet advice). For coccidiosis, use toltrazuril. Keep the pen dry and clean. Disinfect with 1% bleach. For pneumonia, look for coughing and rapid breathing. Improve ventilation and reduce dust. Use antibiotics if needed. For anaemia (pale skin), inject iron dextran at 3 days old (200 mg per piglet). Also, give vitamin E and selenium injection at 3 days if your soil is deficient. Deworm at 2 weeks with fenbendazole or ivermectin. Vaccinate according to local diseases: usually at 3 weeks for mycoplasma, at 4 weeks for circovirus. Keep records of all treatments. Mortality target: under 10% from birth to weaning. If you lose more, check your management. Weigh piglets weekly. A piglet that doesn't gain weight is sick. Isolate and treat early. Always wash hands and boots before entering the nursery. Use footbaths with disinfectant. Quarantine new pigs for 2 weeks. These steps save lives.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Piglet Performance
lessons.body: Good records help you spot problems and improve. You need a notebook or a simple record sheet. For each litter, record: sow ID, farrowing date, number born alive, number stillborn, number mummified, birth weights of each piglet (or average), and any deformities. Then record daily: deaths (with date and cause), treatments given, and feed intake. Weekly: weigh a sample of piglets (at least 5) to track growth. At weaning, record weaning date, number weaned, average weaning weight, and any health issues. Also record feed used per pen. Use a simple code: e.g., 'D' for diarrhoea, 'R' for respiratory, 'C' for crushing. At the end of each batch, calculate: pre-weaning mortality rate = (number born alive - number weaned) / number born alive x 100. Target under 10%. Average daily gain = (weaning weight - birth weight) / days. For a 4-week weaning, target 200-250 g per day. Feed conversion ratio = total feed eaten / total weight gain. Target 1.5-2.0 kg feed per kg gain. Keep records for at least 2 years. Compare batches. If mortality rises, check environment, nutrition, and disease. If growth is slow, check feed quality and health. Use records to decide which sows to keep. A sow that consistently weans few or small piglets should be culled. Share records with your vet or extension officer. They can help you interpret. Even a simple exercise book works. Write with a pen, not pencil. Keep it in a dry place. At the end of the year, you will see patterns and make better decisions.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do for a newborn piglet?
options: B) Clear mucus from its mouth and nose
quiz.explanation: Clearing the airway is the priority to allow breathing.

quiz.q: What temperature should the farrowing pen be for the first week?
quiz.explanation: Newborn piglets cannot regulate body temperature and need warmth around 30-32Â°C.

quiz.q: Why do you clip needle teeth?
options: A) To prevent injury to the sow and other piglets
B) To help the piglet eat
D) To make the piglet grow faster
quiz.explanation: Needle teeth are sharp and can cut the sow's udder and other piglets' faces.

quiz.q: What is the ideal birth weight for a piglet?
quiz.explanation: A healthy piglet weighs between 1.2 and 1.8 kg at birth.

quiz.q: How soon after birth must a piglet receive colostrum?
quiz.explanation: Antibodies in colostrum can only be absorbed for about 6 hours after birth.

quiz.q: What is the best way to ensure all piglets get colostrum if there are more piglets than teats?
options: D) Wait for the sow to produce more milk
quiz.explanation: Split-suckling ensures each piglet gets access to colostrum.

quiz.q: Which teats give the most milk?
options: D) All teats give equal milk
quiz.explanation: Front teats have more milk, so small piglets should be put on them.

quiz.q: What should you do if a sow rejects a piglet?
options: B) Foster it onto another sow
D) Put it with older pigs
quiz.explanation: Fostering onto a sow that has just farrowed is best for the piglet's survival.

quiz.q: What is creep feed?
options: B) Highly digestible feed for piglets
quiz.explanation: Creep feed is specially formulated for young piglets to help them transition to solid food.

quiz.q: At what age should you start offering creep feed?
quiz.explanation: Piglets can start nibbling creep feed from about 7 days old.

quiz.q: What is the ideal protein content in creep feed?
quiz.explanation: Creep feed should have 20-22% protein for good growth.

quiz.q: What is the most stressful time for piglets?
quiz.explanation: Weaning involves separation from the sow and a change in diet, causing stress.

quiz.q: What is fence-line weaning?
options: A) Weaning piglets in a different building
B) Keeping piglets in the same pen but separated by a fence
quiz.explanation: Fence-line weaning allows piglets to see and smell the sow, reducing stress.

quiz.q: How should you transition from creep feed to nursery diet?
quiz.explanation: Gradual mixing prevents digestive upset.

quiz.q: What temperature should the nursery be in the first week after weaning?
quiz.explanation: Weaned piglets need warmth, around 28-30Â°C initially.

quiz.q: How much space does each piglet need in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: Each piglet requires 0.3-0.4 square metres for comfort and growth.

quiz.q: What is a sign of poor ventilation in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia smell indicates poor ventilation and can harm piglets' lungs.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of farrowing rails?
options: A) To keep the sow in place
B) To provide a safe zone for piglets
quiz.explanation: Farrowing rails create a safe area where piglets can escape being crushed by the sow.

quiz.q: What is the first treatment for a piglet with diarrhoea?
quiz.explanation: Rehydration is critical to replace lost fluids and electrolytes.

quiz.q: At what age should piglets receive iron injection?
quiz.explanation: Iron dextran is given at 3 days to prevent anaemia.

quiz.q: What is the target pre-weaning mortality rate?
quiz.explanation: With good management, mortality should be below 10%.

quiz.q: What does a feed conversion ratio of 1.8 mean?
options: A) 1.8 kg feed per kg gain
B) 1.8 kg gain per kg feed
quiz.explanation: Feed conversion ratio is feed intake divided by weight gain.

quiz.q: Why should you record birth weights?
options: A) To know which piglets to cull
B) To track growth and identify weak piglets
quiz.explanation: Birth weights help monitor piglet health and growth progress.

quiz.q: What is the best way to identify piglets?
quiz.explanation: Ear notching or tagging provides permanent identification.

quiz.q: What should you do with a sow that consistently weans few piglets?
quiz.explanation: Poor performing sows should be culled to improve herd productivity.

quiz.q: What is the ideal weaning weight at 4 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Piglets should weigh 6-8 kg at 4 weeks with good management.

quiz.q: How often should you change bedding in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: Daily change keeps the pen dry and reduces disease.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a hospital pen?
options: A) To isolate sick or small piglets
quiz.explanation: A hospital pen provides special care for vulnerable piglets.

quiz.q: What should you do before new piglets arrive in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: All these steps prepare a clean, warm environment.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of keeping good records?
options: B) To make better management decisions
quiz.explanation: Records help identify problems and track performance.
